Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 77, verses 1–7:

﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾ ﴿and those that blow violently in gusts﴾ ﴿and those that spread [clouds] widely﴾ ﴿and those that separate [truth from falsehood] decisively﴾ ﴿and those that deliver the reminder﴾ ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾ ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is surely going to occur﴾

It is an oath by great created things that indicate the great knowledge and power of God, the Exalted.

The purpose of this oath is to emphasize the report, and the lengthening of the oath serves to arouse the listener's eagerness to receive what is sworn to.

The attributes described may refer to one single kind, and they may refer to two kinds or more of great created things. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) followed the view that all those sworn by are angels.

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) did not differ that ﴿those that deliver the reminder﴾ refers to the angels.

Al-Jumhur said: al-'Asifat (those that blow violently) are the winds, and al-Tabari did not report any dissent on this. Al-Qurtubi said: it has been said that al-'Asifat are the angels.

As for al-Farriqat (those that separate), al-Tabari did not report anything except that they are the angels or the messengers. Al-Qurtubi reported from Mujahid that they are the winds.

Regarding the other attributes apart from these, the interpreters differed: some took them to be angels, and others took them to be winds.

As for al-Mursalat (those sent forth), Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, Muqatil, Abu Salih, al-Kalbi and Masruq said they are the angels. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said they are the winds, and this is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud; perhaps he permits both interpretations, and this is the more fitting given that it is conjoined with the particle fa'.

As for al-Nashirat (those that spread), Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Abu Salih said they are the angels. Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid said they are the winds, and this is also reported from Abu Salih.

What results from this is that God swore by two kinds of His great created things, like His saying ﴿By the sky with its constellations, and the promised Day﴾ [al-Buruj: 1], and the like of this recurs in the Qur'an.

Regarding their distribution, it is apparent that the attributes conjoined by fa' belong to the kind of that to which they are conjoined, while those conjoined by waw are more likely attributes of another kind.

Thus the more probable view is that al-Mursalat and al-'Asifat are two attributes of the winds, and that what follows them are attributes of the angels, and the second waw is for conjunction and is not the particle of oath. The reason for combining these two kinds in the oath is that both are among the celestial existents, since the basic principle of conjunction with waw is that the conjoined item is a different entity from that which it is conjoined to. What comes contrary to this is against the norm, like the verse of the poet recited by al-Farra':

To the king, the lion-like and the son of the valiant, and the lion of the battalion in the crowd.

He meant the attributes of one praised person.

Let us now discuss these attributes:

As for al-Mursalat, if it is taken as an attribute of the angels, the intended meaning is those sent to the messengers and prophets, like Jibril in his sending down of revelation and other angels whom God sends to some of His prophets with instruction, news or support, as in His saying, exalted is He, about Zakariyya ﴿The angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39], etc.; or al-Mursalat are those who carry out God's command concerning punishment, like the messengers to the people of Lut. And ʿurfan (in gusts) is a circumstantial clause conveying the meaning of an eloquent simile, i.e., like the mane of a horse in the succession of its hairs one after another. It is said: "They are like the mane of the hyena" when they gather together, and it is said: "They came as one mane." It is suitable for describing both the angels and the wind.

ʿUrfan has also been explained as a noun, i.e., the hair on the neck of the horse, and its accusative is as a circumstantial clause in the manner of eloquent simile, i.e., like the mane in the succession of one part after another. It has also been explained as a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., "known" (the opposite of "unknown"), and that its accusative is as an object of purpose, i.e., for the sake of guidance and righteousness.

(Fa al-'asifat) is a consequence of al-mursalat, i.e., they are sent and so they blow violently. The term al-'asf is applied to the strength of the blowing of the wind. If by al-mursalat is meant the attribute of winds, then al-'asf is literal; and if by al-mursalat is meant the attribute of angels, then al-'asf is a metaphor for the swiftness of their descent, likened to the violence of the wind, in the eagerness for rapid arrival in carrying out what they were commanded.

(ʿAsfan) is an emphatic of the attribute, emphasizing the affirmation of the attribute, since there is no reason to intend removing the possibility of metaphor.

Al-nashr: its literal meaning is the opposite of folding, and its use is frequent metaphorically for manifesting and clarifying, and for bringing out.

So al-nashirat, if taken as an attribute of the angels, may be their spreading of revelation, i.e., their repeated descent for that purpose, and the spreading may be a metonymy for clarity, i.e., with clear laws.

If it is taken as an attribute of the winds, it is the spreading of clouds through the atmosphere; its conjunction with waw rather than fa' is then to indicate that it is conjoined to al-mursalat and not to al-'asifat, because violent blowing is a harmful state while spreading is a state of benefit.

The discussion of the emphasis of "nashran" and its tanwin is like the discussion of "'asfan."

Al-farq: it is the distinguishing between things. If it is an attribute of the angels, it is suitable for the real distinction, like the separation of the people of Paradise from the people of Hellfire on the Day of Reckoning, and the separation of the nations punished in this world from those whom God saved from punishment, like the people of Nuh from Nuh, 'Ad from Hud, the people of Lut from Lut and his family except his wife; and it is suitable for the metaphorical distinction, namely that they bring the revelation which separates truth from falsehood, and faith from disbelief.

If it is taken as an attribute of the winds, it is one of the effects of spreading, i.e., their separating the clusters of clouds over the lands.

Because the distinction in both its meanings branches off from spreading in its meanings, al-farriqat is conjoined to al-nashirat by fa'.

It is emphasized with the absolute object just as what precedes it was emphasized with "'asfan" and "nashran," and its tanwin is likewise.

Al-muljiyat: the angels who convey the revelation, which is the reminder.

Al-ilqa' is used metaphorically for conveying the reminder from the higher world to the people of the earth, likening it to the casting of something from the hand to the ground.

The casting of the reminder is the conveying of admonitions to the messengers so that they convey them to the people, and this casting branches off from distinction, because they assign each reminder to whoever is in need of it: the reminder of disbelievers with threat and warning of punishment, and the reminder of believers with praise and promise of bliss.

This is the meaning of ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾. Al-'udhr: the informing of the acceptance of the faith of believers after disbelief, and of the repentance of the repentant after sin.

Al-nudhur: the verbal noun of anzara, when he warns.

"'Udhran" was read by the majority with the dhal sukun, and Rawh from Ya'qub read it with damma on the dhal following the vowel of the ʿayn.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read "nudhuran" with damma on the dhal, which is its predominant form.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim and Khalaf read it with sukun on the dhal, according to the two aforementioned readings of "'udhuran," and on both readings it is a verbal noun meaning warning.

"'Udhran aw nudhran" is in the accusative as a substitution of inclusion from "dhikran." The "aw" in "aw nudhuran" is for division.

The clause ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is surely going to occur﴾ is the answer of the oath, and it was reinforced with inna for strengthening the confirmation of the occurrence of the answer.

"Innama" consists of two words: "inna," which is the particle of emphasis, and "ma," the relative pronoun; it is not the "innama" which is the particle of restriction, in which "ma" is superfluous. These were written joined, "inna" with "ma," because they did not distinguish in the orthography between the two cases, and orthography is a convention; the orthography of the Mushaf is a established practice in the copies, while we write them separated in tafsir and elsewhere.

"Ma tu'aduna" is the resurrection for recompense, and they know the referent, therefore it is expressed with the relative form.

The address is to the polytheists, i.e., what God has promised you of punishment after resurrection is certainly going to occur, even if you doubt it or deny it.

Al-waqi': the established. The original sense of al-waqi' is that which has fallen to the ground, and it is borrowed for a thing that has been realized, by way of likening it to what is settled.

The address is to the polytheists, i.e., what God has promised you of punishment after resurrection is certainly going to occur, even if you doubt it or deny it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 77, verses 8–14:**

﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾ ﴿and when the sky is split open﴾ ﴿and when the mountains are blown away﴾ ﴿and when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾ ﴿for what Day have they been postponed?﴾ ﴿For the Day of Decision﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾

The *fa'* (فاء) here is for *tafri'* (تفريع, consequence), building on the verse ﴿What you are promised will surely occur﴾ (al-Mursalat: 7). Because the verse affirms that the Resurrection will occur, and the addressees denied it and used the delay in its occurrence as an excuse, it explains to them what will happen before it, adding to its awesomeness for them. The warning that it is deferred until those great events take place contains a figurative *kinayah* (كناية, implicature) confirming that it will certainly happen, since reporting the signs of the arrival of what they are promised necessarily entails warning against taking it lightly. For this reason these reports are concluded with the words ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ (al-Mursalat: 34).

The word *idha* (إذا) is repeated at the beginning of the clauses coordinated with this clause after coordinating particles, while the coordinating particle makes it unnecessary to repeat *idha*, as in ﴿So when the sight is dazzled, and the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and moon are joined, on that Day man will say...﴾ (al-Qiyamah: 7) and so on. This serves to emphasize the content of each of these clauses, so that each content stands independently as a sign of the occurrence of what they are promised.

The *tams* (طمس, obliteration) of the stars is the cessation of their light. The light of most of what appears to people of the stars is caused by the reflection of the rays of the sun upon them when the light of the sun is hidden from the dark side of the earth. Thus the obliteration of the stars implies the obliteration of the sun's light, that is, the cessation of its burning, either by its heat cooling, or by a grey layer covering its surface due to eruptions from within, or by its colliding with other celestial bodies because the system of gravitation is disrupted, so that it crumbles and breaks into pieces and its burning ceases.

The meaning of *furijat* (فرجت, split open) is that what was joined in its structure separates. It is said: "the door was *furija*" when he opened it, and *al-furjah* (الفرجة) is an opening in a wall or the like. If by "the sky" is meant the genus that truly encompasses all the heavens, in the manner of true generality, or what encompasses the well-known heavens, in the manner of customary generality, namely the seven heavens which the astronomers call the wandering planets, then the splitting of the heavens could be the occurrence of great fissures in the planets, in addition to the obliteration of their light.

If by "the sky" is meant a specific known individual, namely what we observe as the blue dome during the day, which is the sphere of air, then the meaning of *furijat* is the corruption of the elements of the atmosphere, such that in it there become streaks of varying colors that appear like cracks in the sphere of air, as in the words of God Most High ﴿When the sky is split asunder﴾ (al-Inshiqaq: 1). All of this leads to the annihilation of the worldly world with its whole order and the totality of its bodies.

*Al-naff* (النسف, blowing away) is the uprooting of the parts of a thing from one another and scattering them, like demolition.

The *nasf* of the mountains is their crushing and their becoming scattered dust, as God Most High said ﴿And the mountains will be like poured-out heaps of sand﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 14).

The construction of these three verbs in the passive voice is because the intended purpose is to take heed of the occurrence of the action rather than specifying its agent, although it is known that its agent is God Most High, since no one else is capable of it.

The clause ﴿and when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾ is coordinated with the preceding clauses, so it specifies a time that will occur, and it is among those whose content is made a sign of the occurrence of what they are promised. Therefore its content must be something yet to occur. The composition of this clause contains obscurity and subtlety. As for *uqqitat* (أقّتت), its origin is *wuqqitat* (وقّتت) with a *waw* at its beginning. It is said *waqqata waqtan*, when he set a time for some work, derived from *al-waqt* (الوقت), which means time. When it is constructed in the passive, the *waw* takes a *damma*, and this is a necessary *damma*, to avoid the *damma* in ﴿and do not forget the bounty among you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 237), because the *damma* on the *waw* is an incidental *damma*. So it was permissible to replace it with a *hamza*, because a *damma* on a *waw* is heavy, so one turns from the *waw* to the *hamza*. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *uqqitat* with a *hamza* and a shadda on the *qaf*. Abu 'Amr alone read it with a *waw* and shadda on the *qaf*, and Abu Ja'far read it with a *waw* and without shadda on the *qaf*.

The nature of *idha* is that it pertains to future time, so this setting of a time for the messengers is a time-setting that will occur in the future, and it is a sign that what they are promised will occur together with the other signs.

There is no disagreement that *uqqitat* is derived from *al-waqt*, as you have just learned. The original derivation of this passive verb is that its meaning would be: "they were made a time," and this is the original way of attributing the verb to its nominative subject. It may also mean: "a time was set for them," by way of omission and transitivization.

Since *idha* is an adverb of future time, and the appointing of the messengers had already occurred before the revelation of this verse, the interpretation of *uqqitat* is necessarily as: its time has come, that is, the appointed time for the messengers, which is the time about which God informed them, that they should warn their nations that it will arrive in an unspecified future. This is supported by His words ﴿for what Day have they been postponed? For the Day of Decision﴾, since postponement explains appointment.

The early exegetes (al-mufassirun al-awwalun) differed in their views on the meaning of this verse. From Ibn 'Abbas: *uqqitat* means *jumi'at*, that is, gathered for the Day of Resurrection, as God Most High said ﴿the Day when God will gather the messengers﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 109). From Mujahid and al-Nakha'i: *uqqitat* means *ujjilat* (أجّلت, postponed). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: that is, the Day of Judgment and Decision was made its time.

In *al-Kashshaf* he said: "The preferable view is that the meaning of *wuqqitat* is that they reached their appointed time, which they were awaiting, namely the Day of Resurrection." End. This is explicit that *wuqqita* is said with the meaning "brought at the appointed time," and the commentators on *al-Kashshaf* accepted it, although this meaning is overlooked in some lexicons or concealed obscurely in others.

According to this view, the words ﴿for what Day have they been postponed﴾ would be a new independent clause (isti'naf), and *ayy* (أيّ) would be treated as an interrogative noun used for magnification, as the majority of commentators who stated it explicitly followed, without ambiguity. What appears to me is that *ayy* should be a relative (mawsulah) indicating glorification and magnitude, which is what is expressed by the term "indicating the meaning of perfection." It would be an adjective to an omitted noun, indicated by what *ayy* is annexed to, and its estimated form is: "for a day of what day," that is, for a great day. The meaning of *uqqitat* would then be "its appointed time arrived, which was set for it," and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, "gathered." In *al-Lisan*, from al-Farra': *uqqitat* means "gathered at its time," and this is the saying of God Most High ﴿the Day God gathers the messengers﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 109), and His words ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ (al-Nisa': 41).

The *lam* in His words ﴿for what Day have they been postponed﴾ would be the *lam* of causation (lam al-ta'lil), meaning: they were gathered for the sake of the day to which they were postponed. The clause *ujjilat* is an adjective to *yawm*, and the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is omitted due to its clarity, meaning: they were postponed to it.

His words ﴿for the Day of Decision﴾ are a substitute (badal) for ﴿for what Day have they been postponed﴾, with the preposition by which the substituted-from noun is governed repeated, like His words ﴿it will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 114), meaning: the messengers were brought to a great day, which is the Day of Decision.

It is apparent that the substituted-from noun and the substitute are two indications of the response (jawab) of *idha* in His words ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾ and so on, since it is understood that the meaning is: when all that has been mentioned has occurred, then that is the occurrence of what you are promised.

The clause ﴿for what Day have they been postponed, for the Day of Decision﴾ has already been explained with the sound interpretation of its meaning. Some exegetes made it a quotation of an omitted saying: "It is said on the Day of Resurrection," but there is no need for this.

*Al-Fasl* (الفصل, decision) is the distinguishing of truth from falsehood through judgment and recompense, for by this confusion, ambiguity, and deception that the people of error had in this world disappear, and realities become clear as they actually are.

The clause ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to *yawm al-fasl*, and the *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance. The linking element for the circumstantial clause is the repetition of the name of the subject of the circumstance in place of its pronoun, like ﴿The Striking Calamity, what is the Striking Calamity?﴾ (al-Qari'ah: 1). The original would be: "and what will make you know what it is," and it was made apparent in place of the pronoun to strengthen the evocation of the Day of Decision, with the intent of magnifying it.

*Ma* (ما) is an interrogative, a subject (mubtada'), and *adraka* (أدراك) is its predicate, meaning: "I will inform you." And ﴿what the Day of Decision is?﴾ is an interrogative clause, to which the verb *adraka* is suspended from acting on two objects. The interrogative *ma* is also a subject, and *yawm al-fasl* is its predicate. Both interrogatives are used with the meaning of magnification and amazement.

His words ﴿for the Day of Decision﴾ are a substitute (badal) for ﴿for what Day have they been postponed﴾, with the preposition by which the substituted-from noun is governed repeated, like His words ﴿it will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 114), meaning: the messengers were brought to a great day, which is the Day of Decision.

The clause ﴿for what Day have they been postponed, for the Day of Decision﴾ has already been explained with the sound interpretation of its meaning. Some exegetes made it a quotation of an omitted saying: "It is said on the Day of Resurrection," but there is no need for this.

**Translation:**

Taking this sentence together with the similar sentences that come after it in this surah requires that it be treated as a new, independent statement (*istinaf*). Its purpose is to warn the polytheists who hear the Qur'an and to inspire awe of the Day of Judgment (*yawm al-fasl*, the Day of Decision) in their hearts, so that they will beware of it. In meaning, it is connected to the sentence ﴿Indeed, what you are promised will surely occur﴾ [al-Mursalat: 7] in the way that the parts of a composition are connected. Thus the position of the sentence ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ is that of the beginning of a new discourse, while the position of the sentence ﴿When the stars are obliterated﴾ [al-Mursalat: 8] is that of what follows. It was placed first only to indicate the meaning of a conditional. By changing the arrangement in this way, the sentence ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ has come to function as a concluding statement (*tadhyil*), and so this composition contains an excellent style and wondrous meanings.

Some exegetes made this sentence the response (*jawab*) of the conditional particle *idha* (when), meaning that *idha* is connected to the stability implied in the predicate, which is "for the deniers." The sense is: when such-and-such occurs, woe befalls the deniers. This serves as an explanation of ﴿Indeed, what you are promised will surely occur﴾ [al-Mursalat: 7], and so it reinforces the threat. This view is not affected by the objection that the response lacks the connecting *fa'* (then), because the response of *idha* is a formal response, and what is really connected to *idha* is treated as a response in meaning.

Furthermore, this sentence is capable of conveying both the sense of a declarative statement and the sense of an expression of invocation (*insha'*), because the structure "woe to him" (*wayl lahu*) is commonly used as an expression of invocation.

*Al-wayl* means the utmost evil and harm.

According to the first view, the intended meaning of "the deniers" is those who denied the Qur'an. According to the second view, the meaning of the sentence includes all who denied the messengers and what they brought. Through this generality, the sentence fulfills the function of a concluding statement. This includes the polytheists who denied the Qur'an and the Resurrection, since they are the intended audience of these admonitions and the ones to whom this discourse is addressed. Thus they are addressed by the words ﴿Indeed, what you are promised will surely occur﴾ [al-Mursalat: 7].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 77, verse 16:

﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), addressed to the polytheists present who denied the Resurrection. It is an interjection (i'tiraD) placed between parts of the speech addressed to the people of polytheism at the gathering (al-mahshar).

It also contains an argument directed at the polytheists of the worldly life: that God took vengeance upon those among the nations who disbelieved in the Day of Resurrection, both those who came before and those who came after, so that they would beware lest there befall them what befell those former and latter peoples.

The interrogative (istifham) here is for affirmation (taqrir), serving as proof for the possibility of the Resurrection by way of analogical reasoning (qiyas al-tamthil).

By "the former ones" (al-awwalin) is meant those described by priority, that is, precedence in time, and every generation among them is preceded by a generation that disbelieved.

The definite article in al-awwalin is the definite article of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), and by "the former ones" is meant all the nations of polytheism who existed before the polytheists of the age of prophethood.

Destruction (al-ihlak) means annihilation and causing to die. The destruction of the former ones has two conditions: an unusual condition arising from God's wrath, namely total destruction (ihlak al-isti'sal), like the destruction of 'Ad and Thamud; and an ordinary condition, which is what God has established as the order of this world of life and death.

Both conditions may be intended here. As for the unusual condition, it is a reminder of the evidence that God is not pleased with those who denied the Resurrection. As for the ordinary condition, it is proof that He who gives life to people causes them to die, so it is not difficult for Him to restore their life.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 77, verses 25–27:

﴿Did We not make the earth a container﴾ ﴿for the living and the dead?﴾ ﴿And We placed therein firm mountains and gave you sweet water to drink.﴾

This statement comes in the same manner as its predecessors, without a conjunction (ʿatf), because it follows the method of repetition for the purpose of rebuke. It is a reminder to them of what Allah has bestowed upon them by creating the earth with what is in it of benefits for them, as He said (﴿an enjoyment for you and your cattle﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 33]).

The point of the favour (al-imtinan) is His saying "for the living," while His saying "and the dead" is a complement (tatmim) and an inclusion (idmaj).

Kifat (کفات) is a noun for that in which something is gathered (yukfat), that is, collected and held together in it. It is a noun formed on the pattern fi'al from kafata, meaning he gathered. From this the receptacle is called kifat, just as that which holds a thing is called wi'a' (container), and that which holds a thing together is called al-dimam.

"Ahyaʾan" (living) is the object (maf'ul) of "kifatan," because "kifatan" carries the meaning of a verb, as if it were said: gathering (kafitatan) the living. Some say it is governed by a verb understood from "kifatan," and all of this is close in meaning.

"Wa-amwatan" (and the dead) is conjoined to it, and it is an inclusion and a complement, because in it is the observed inseparability between the living and the dead, which indicates that life is the purpose of creation.

This is a reminder to them to acknowledge the observed conditions on the earth, which indicate Allah's exclusive divinity (infirad Allah bi'l-ilahiyya).

The tanwin of (﴿ahyaʾan wa-amwatan﴾) is for magnification, intending multiplicity; for this reason they were not brought in with the definite article. The benefit of mentioning these two plurals is what their meanings contain of reminder of life and death.

The discourse has addressed the establishment of resurrection (al-ba'th) with three proofs:

First: the condition of the perished nations in their extinction.

Second: the condition of the creation of man.

Third: the destiny of all to the earth. In all of this is a refutation of their claim that the resurrection is impossible, since they asserted its impossibility; their claim is refuted by establishing its possibility, for once possibility is established, impossibility is nullified, and nothing remains but to consider the evidences that favour the occurrence of that possible matter.

In the verse is a favour that makes the earth suitable for burying the dead. Allah inspired this to the son of Adam when he killed his brother, as mentioned earlier in Surat al-Ma'idah. From the verse is derived the obligation of burial in the earth, unless that is impossible, such as one who dies on a ship far from the anchorages of land, or who cannot be anchored, or whose anchoring would harm the passengers, or where the decay of the corpse is feared; in such cases it is cast into the sea and weighted with something so that it sinks to the bottom of the water. Accordingly, it is not permissible to burn the dead, as the Magians of India do, and as some of the Romans used to do, nor to leave it for birds of prey, as the Magians of Persia used to do. The people of the Jahiliyya used to boast of the dead one whom beasts or hyenas devour, namely the one who dies slain in the wilderness. Ta'abbata Sharran said:

Do not bury me, for my burial is forbidden to you,
but leave me to the mother of ʿAmir (the hyena).

This is from the ignorance of the Jahiliyya and ingratitude for blessings.

Ibn al-Qasim, from the companions of Malik, argued from this verse that the grave is a protected place (hirz), and so he required the amputation of the hand of one who steals from a grave a shroud or what amounts to a quarter of a dinar. Malik said: the grave is a sanctuary (hiwaz) for the dead, just as the house is a sanctuary for the living.

In Mafatih al-Ghayb, from the tafsir of al-Qaffal, it is reported that Rabi'a used this verse as evidence for that.

Al-rawasi is the plural of ra's (peak), i.e., firm mountains, that is, fixed in the earth. Al-Samaw'al said:

Its root has settled beneath the soil, and it rose high with a branch unreachable, lofty, toward the star.

It was pluralized on the pattern fawa'il because it is used as an adjective for a masculine non-rational noun. This is a favour of the creation of mountains, for they used to take refuge in them and benefit from what is in them of pasture and trees. Allah said (﴿And the mountains He set firm as an enjoyment for you and your cattle﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 32]).

Al-shamikhat means the elevated ones.

﴿And gave you sweet water to drink﴾ is conjoined because of the connection with the mention of the mountains, for water flows down from them, running in their lower parts, which are the valleys, and it settles in pools, basins and small lakes.

Al-furat is sweet water, and it is rain water.

The tanwin of (shamikhat) and (﴿ma'an furatan﴾) is for magnification, since this indicates the greatness of power.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 77, verse 30–31:

﴿Depart toward that which you used to deny.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 29] ﴿Depart toward a shade of three branches,﴾ ﴿neither shading nor availing against the blaze.﴾

This is an address to the deniers on the Day of Gathering (yawm al-hashr), so it is the object of an omitted saying (maqul qawl mahdhuf), which is indicated by the form of the address with "depart," without there being a addressee who is being commanded at this moment.

Page 435
The implied pronoun with the omitted saying refers to the deniers, meaning: it is said to the deniers.
The command for their departure is used in the sense of compulsion (taskhir), because the angels of punishment drive them forcibly.

"That which they used to deny" is Jahannam (Hell), and it is expressed by a relative pronoun with its relative clause because the clause contains a rebuke of their error and misguidance, in the manner of the words of 'Abdah ibn al-Tabib:

Indeed those whom you see as your brothers, the cure for the rage in their breasts is that you be felled.

The clause "Depart toward a shade..." to its end is either a badal al-ishtimal (partial substitution) or a badal al-mutabaqa (full substitution) for the clause "Depart toward that which you used to deny" [al-Mursalat: 29]. The verb "depart" (inṭaliqū) is repeated in the manner of repetition, for the purpose of rebuke, humiliation and repulsion, and for this purpose the verb "depart" and the preposition "ilā" are repeated.

The apparent construction would have been: "Depart toward that which you used to deny, a shade of three branches," so repeating the governing verb in the substitute is for emphasis in a context of reproach.

By "shade" is meant the smoke of Jahannam, because of its density; it is expressed as "shade" in mockery of them, because they long for a shade under whose coolness they might take refuge.

"Shade" is given in the singular here because that smoke is made for them in one place, so that they are crowded together beneath it, since that crowding increases their pain.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read the second "inṭaliqū" with a kasra on the lam, like the first "inṭaliqū." Ruways from Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the lam, in the form of the past tense, meaning that they were commanded to depart toward the Fire, so they departed toward its smoke. The reason it is not joined with fa' is the intention of resumption (isti'naf), so that it is another report about their state.

Al-shu'ab (branches): the plural noun of shu'bah, which is a group of a thing and a portion of it, i.e., of three groups or portions. By it is meant portions of the smoke, for when the fire's blaze grows intense, its smoke rises from its two ends and its middle, because of the intensity of its compression in emerging from it.

Page 436
So the smoke is described as having three branches, because it will be so on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said regarding the reason for this: one branch of it is on the right, one branch on the left, and one branch above. Al-Fakhr said: I say this is not unlikely, because anger is on his right, desire on his left, and the satanic power is in his brain, and the source of all the afflictions arising from man in his beliefs and in his deeds is nothing but these three. It is possible to say that there are here three degrees, which are: sense, imagination, and illusion. They prevent the soul from being illumined by the lights of the world of holiness, end quote.

Al-zalil: the strong in its shade. A descriptive form is derived from its name to convey its perfection in what is intended from it, like: a night that is dark (laylun alyal), and poetry that is poetic (shi'run sha'ir), meaning it is not like the shade of the believers. God the Exalted said: "And We shall admit them into a shade, a deep shade" [al-Nisa': 57]. In this there is a disappointment for them, and it has the sense of the words of God the Exalted: "And a shade of black smoke, neither cool nor generous" [al-Waqi'ah: 43].

With this, it strips this shade of the properties of shades, because the nature of a shade is to relieve the one who takes refuge in it from the pain of heat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 77, verses 32–33:

﴿Indeed, it hurls sparks like a palace,﴾ ﴿as if they were yellow camels.﴾

It is possible that this is part of what is said to the deniers, to whom it was said (﴿Go to that which you used to deny.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 29]). After they have despaired of anything that would relieve them of the punishment they suffer, and it is said to them, "Go to the smoke of Jahannam," perhaps at that moment they see Jahannam hurling its sparks, and the sight terrifies them. Or they see it from a distance, where things are not clearly distinguishable, and signs of their expectation that they will reach it appear upon them, so they are made to feel even greater terror and dread. Then it is said to them: "Indeed, Jahannam hurls sparks like a palace, as if they were yellow camels."

It is also possible that this is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) in the midst of describing their condition, or at the end of describing their condition.

[Page 437]

The pronoun in "innaha" ("indeed it") refers to Jahannam, which is indicated by His saying (﴿that which you used to deny﴾ [al-Mursalat: 29]). This is like what is said to one who is being led to execution who sees a man with a sword in his hand and trembles at the sight: it is said to him, "Indeed, it is the executioner."

The attribution of those descriptions in the report about it serves to increase the terror and dread. If they were seeing those sparks because they were close to them, then describing it to them serves to confirm the terror and dread by combining hearing with seeing. If they were at a distance from it, then the description serves to reveal its dreadful state.

The emphasis of the report with "inna" ("indeed") is for the sake of giving it importance, because at that time they do not doubt it, whether they see it or are told about it.

*Red, its tufts blazing in the darkness,*
*it hurls every spark like a ṭirāf (tent-flap)*

He compared the spark to a ṭirāf, which is a leather tent in size and redness. It seems he intended, with his malice, to surpass the Qur'anic comparison, and out of his boastfulness over the illusion of excelling it that had been made attractive to him, he placed at the beginning of his verse "red" as a preparation for it, a summons to it, and an alert to the listeners to its place. I say: This statement is a bad assumption about al-Ma'arri, for nothing of it is perceived from his speech, and none of those who defamed or blamed him attributed it to him. Al-Zamakhshari added it to the lute of those who harbor resentment, and there is a tone of defamation and insult in it.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: It would have been better for the author of al-Kashshaf not to mention that, that is, because it is a bad assumption without evidence.

And that was considered in relation to animals, and that those movements are voluntary, and all of that is absent from his verse.

The noun yawm is not given tanwin (nunation) because it is annexed to a sentence, just as ḥīn ("time") is annexed. Therefore the subjunctive reading of fa-ya'taḍhirūna is not equal to the nominative, and indeed is not permissible.

This differs from a construction such as (﴿nor will it be decreed against them so that they die﴾ Fatir 35:36), where the negation of decree against them while they are in punishment is intended for its own sake, because it signifies continuance of their punishment. Know that there is no contradiction between this verse and the verses that indicate that they do offer excuses, such as His words (﴿They will say: Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice, so we acknowledge our sins; is there any way out?﴾ Ghafir 40:11), because the time of their speech being negated is the Day of Separation.

As for their speech reported in His words (﴿Our Lord, You caused us to die twice﴾ Ghafir 40:11), that is their shouting in Hell after the end of the Day of Separation. In a similar manner, Ibn 'Abbas answered Nafi' ibn al-Azraq when Nafi' said: "I find in the Qur'an things that contradict one another for me. Upon this is built (﴿So if you have any scheme, then scheme against Me﴾), that is: if you have any scheme today as you had in the world, that is, a scheme against My religion and My Messenger, then do it.

Qur'an 77:45: "Woe on that Day to the deniers."

On the first reading, this sentence (﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾) is a repetition of its counterparts, the same refrain that follows the verse ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be among shades and springs﴾ [al-Mursalat: 41]. The day referred to by "that day" (idh), which carries the nunation of replacement (tanwin al-'iwad), is the day on which that statement was uttered.

As for the second reading, where the sentence follows ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be among shades and springs﴾ [al-Mursalat: 41] and so on, it is connected to that sentence as a contrast to the description of the believers' bliss, which has been expanded at length, by mentioning its opposite for the polytheists in a concise way, derived from the word "woe" (wayl). This creates the contrast of a thing with its opposite, and this sentence serves as an emphasis for its counterparts. The day referred to by "that day" (idh) is a day not mentioned explicitly, but it is implied by the fact that the God-fearing are among shades, springs and fruits, so that one knows that this will be theirs on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 77, verse 46:

﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little; indeed, you are criminals.﴾

This is an address to the polytheists present, those who were addressed by His saying (﴿Indeed, what you are promised is to occur﴾ [al-Mursalat: 7]). It is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) arising from His saying (﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ [al-Mursalat: 44]), since it stirs in the souls of the deniers addressed by these calamitous warnings what frequently occurs to them: that they are in this world in a secure bounty, and that what they are promised is not going to happen. So it was said to them (﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little﴾).

The imperative in His saying (﴿Eat and enjoy﴾) is used to express respite and warning, meaning: your eating and your enjoyment of the pleasures of this world are of no account, because it is a brief enjoyment; then your abode is the everlasting punishment. He, exalted is He, said (﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the lands deceive you. It is a brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196]).

The clause (﴿indeed, you are criminals﴾) is a predicate used in the sense of threat and warning of evil, meaning: your criminality is leading you down to punishment. This is derived from the contrast between their description as criminals and the description of the God-fearing as doers of good, since the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. Thus the clause takes the place of a causal explanation.

The emphasis of the predicate with (inna) is to refute their denial that they are criminals.

Verse 47: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾ It is like its counterpart mentioned a second time in this surah.

It adds to that a particular connection with the clause (﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves a little, [but] you are criminals﴾ [al-Mursalat: 46]) because of what is in (tamatta'u qaliylan, "enjoy yourselves a little") of kinaya (allusion, indirect expression) for anticipating an evil outcome for them. So his saying (﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 49]) falls in the position of explanation (bayan) for that kinaya, meaning: "Eat and enjoy yourselves a little now, and woe to you on the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 77, verse 48:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down.﴾

It is permissible that this be a conjunction (ʿatf) upon his statement (lil-mukadhdhibin, "for the deniers"), and the estimated sense is: "And those who, when it is said to them, 'Bow down,' do not bow down." For the definite article (al-) that enters upon descriptive derived words (al-awsaf al-mushtaqqa) functions mostly as a relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul), and for this reason the grammarians counted it among the relative pronouns and made the descriptive word that the article enters upon a relative clause (silah) for it.

It is also permissible that this be a conjunction upon the sentence "Eat and enjoy yourselves a little" (﴿Kulu wa-tamattaʿu qaliლan﴾ [al-Mursalat: 46]), and the shift from address (khitab) to third person (ghaybah) is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

On both views, it falls under al-idmaj (incorporation), in order to reproach them for their opposition to the Muslims in the acts that indicate inner faith. It is thus a kinayah (metonymy) for their not having faith, because prayer is the pillar of religion (ʿimad al-din). For this reason, the polytheists were described as ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5].

Page 447

The meaning is: when it is said to them, "Believe and bow down," they neither believe nor bow down, just as non-belief is referred to by metonymy, as is reported of them in the Hereafter: ﴿"What brought you into Saqar?" They will say, "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor."﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42–44] and so on to the end.

It is also permissible that this be a conjunction upon his statement ﴿"Indeed, you are criminals"﴾ [al-Mursalat: 46]. In all these views it conveys a threat to them, because it is conjoined either to the denial or to the criminality, and both are a cause for the threat of an evil recompense on the Day of Judgment.

There is no evidence in the verse that the disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Shariah, since the meaning of "those who pray" is not fixed as referring to those who establish the prayer.

This sentence is like its companion sentence that follows it, in that it may be connected to His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48]. The phrase "the deniers" (al-mukadhdhibin) is then an explicit noun used in place of a pronoun (izhar fi maqam al-idmar, the placing of an explicit noun where a pronoun (idmar) would normally stand), intended to describe them as those who deny. The estimated sense is: "Woe on that Day to them, or to you." It is then a threat arising from the clause ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48]. The day indicated by "that Day" (yawma'idhin) is the time implied by "when" (idha) in His words ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down"﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48], the time in which those guilty ones who, when it is said to them, "Bow down," do not bow down, are repaid with woe. That is, they do not believe. Yet this sentence also conveys, along with that, affirmation and emphasis of its counterpart mentioned a second time in this surah.

[Page 448]

The fa' here is *fasihah* (an eloquent fa', one that signals an unstated condition). It points to a hidden condition whose sense is: "If they do not believe in this Qur'an, then in what discourse after it will they believe?" The identity of this hidden element is fixed by what is repeated in the verses "Woe on that day to the deniers" [al-Mursalat: 15], since their denial concerned the Qur'an and what it says about the occurrence of resurrection.

The interrogative is used for *inkar ta'jibi* (a rhetorical denial expressing wonder) at their condition. The meaning is: when they do not affirm the Qur'an despite the clarity of its proof, they will not believe in any other discourse.

[Page 5]

The intended meaning is that the Qur'an is supreme in clarity of indication and in the force of its proof. Those who do not believe in it will not believe in any speech they hear after it.

"Ba'dahu" (after it) may be made a description of *hadith* (discourse). It is then a *zarf mustaqarr* (a stable adverbial complement, one that describes a noun), and "being after" means the lapse of time. The sense is "a discourse that reaches them or is heard after the Qur'an has reached them or been heard." This applies whether the discourse existed before the Qur'an was revealed or appears after it. The meaning is not that they believe in a discourse that came before the Qur'an, such as the Torah, the Gospel, and other admonitions and reports. Rather, the meaning is that they do not believe in any other discourse after failing to believe in the Qur'an, because no speech reaches them that is clearer in indication and proof than the Qur'an.

It is also permissible for "ba'dahu" to be connected to "yu'minun" (they believe). It is then a *zarf laghw* (a loose adverbial complement, one that does not describe a noun), and the word *hadith* remains negated without the qualification that it comes after the Qur'an. The meaning is: they do not believe, after the Qur'an, in every discourse.

The pronoun in "ba'dahu" refers to the Qur'an, although nothing preceding it in this surah indicates it, so that it could serve as its antecedent. It is nevertheless treated as though already mentioned, because it is constantly before their minds on every day of the Prophet's (ﷺ) call to them.

A parallel of this verse occurred at the end of Surat al-A'raf, so add it to what is said here.

It is also permissible for the pronoun in "ba'dahu" to refer to the saying derived from "And when it is said to them, 'Bow down,' they do not bow down" [al-Mursalat: 48]. Their being commanded to bow, which is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for faith, was through the sayings of the Qur'an.

In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful

Surat al-Naba'

This surah is called Surat al-Naba' in most mushafs, books of tafsir, and books of Sunnah, because the word *al-naba'* (the tidings) occurs at its beginning.

In some mushafs, in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah, and in al-Kashshaf, it is called Surat "'Amma yatasa'aluna" (About what are they asking one another?). In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi, it is named Surat "'Amma," meaning without the addition of "yatasa'aluna," naming it after the first sentence in it.

It is also called Surat al-Tasa'ul (the Surah of Questioning), because "yatasa'aluna" occurs at its beginning. It is also called Surat al-Mu'sirat (the Surah of the Clouds that Release Rain), because of God's words in it: "And We send down from the clouds water pouring forth" [al-Naba': 14]. These are five names. Al-Itqan limited itself to four names: 'Amma, al-Naba', al-Tasa'ul, and al-Mu'sirat.

It is a Meccan surah by consensus.

Jabir ibn Zayd counted it as the eightieth surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat al-Ma'arij and before Surat al-Nazi'at.

What is related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan implies that this surah was revealed at the beginning of the mission (*al-ba'th*). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "When the Qur'an was revealed, the Quraysh used to sit and talk among themselves. Some of them affirmed it and some denied it. So there was revealed: 'About what are they asking one another?' [al-Naba': 1]."

From al-Hasan: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, they began to ask one another. So God revealed: 'About what are they asking one another? About the great tidings' [al-Naba': 1–2]," meaning the great news.

Those who counted its verses among the people of Medina, Syria, and Basra counted forty. The people of Mecca and Kufa counted forty-one verses.

This surah includes a description of the disputing of the polytheists concerning the Qur'an and what it brought that contradicts their beliefs. Among this is the affirmation of resurrection, and the questioning of some of them by others about their opinion on its occurrence, mocking the report of its occurrence.

It also contains a warning against their mockery.

It contains an argument for the possibility of resurrection through the creation of created things greater than the creation of man after his death, and through the first creation of man and his conditions.

It describes the terrors that occur at the resurrection, including the punishment of the transgressors, contrasted with a description of the bliss of the believers.

It describes the Day of Gathering as a warning to those who denied it, and as an indication that they will be punished with a near punishment before the punishment of the Day of Resurrection.

Incorporated into this is that the knowledge of God, may He be exalted, encompasses everything, and among the things are the deeds of people.
